The Trump administration is expected to announce plans soon to raise tariffs on China , the European Union, and 14 other economies, according to two people familiar with the matter.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office is expected to release the results of a months-long tariff investigation into industrial subsidies by the 16 economies in the coming days, according to people who were not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.
They stressed that the timing of the tariff rollout could still change. The White House and USTR did not respond to requests for comment.
Plans for the new tariffs are part of an effort to replace broader duties the administration set last year, which the Supreme Court later struck down . The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.
The tariffs respond to what the White House has called excessive manufacturing output in those countries, boosted by subsidies, that has flooded the market with lower-priced goods that undercut American companies.
The anticipated action is a second step in the administration’s efforts to replace the duties announced in April 2025, which the Supreme Court ruled unconstitutional in February. In July, the White House slapped 60 trading partners with levies of 10% to 12.5%, charging that they have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.
This latest move demonstrates that the Trump administration is still willing to impose import taxes despite a sweeping loss for the Republican Party in this month’s midterm elections, fueled largely by affordability concerns as inflation remains elevated .
At the same time, the new duties could test how the Democrats will respond to tariffs imposed unilaterally by Trump. Even with majorities in both the House and Senate , Trump could veto any legislation that overturns or waters down the tariffs.
The excess industrial capacity probes were initiated under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the president to levy tariffs against nations that discriminate against U.S. companies or commerce.
The anticipated tariff levels were not immediately clear, but would be added to the 10% to 12.5% tariffs announced earlier this year.
Many countries, including China, protested those tariffs, which took effect just as the clock ran out on temporary levies Trump had imposed after the Supreme Court in February struck down sweeping “reciprocal” tariffs he levied on nearly every U.S. trade partner.
The expected move comes as Trump visited the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen last week for his third face-to-face engagement with Chinese President Xi Jinping this year. Xi’s expected to travel to Doral , Florida , next month for the Group of 20 Summit, which Trump is hosting.
While Trump has moved to build a closer relationship with Xi, the yawning trade deficit remains a significant irritant in the U.S.-China relationship.
Massive capacity in a slew of Chinese industries, from autos to solar panels, cement and steel manufacturing, has drawn increased attention from Beijing ’s trading partners in recent years.
Although China’s own leaders have prioritized rebalancing the economy, slowing domestic demand has prompted companies to expand into overseas markets. Surging exports pushed China’s trade surplus to a record of nearly $1.2 trillion last year.

articles.title_orig: China Gives First Foreign Crew Member a Ride Into Space
articles.title_zh: China Gives First Foreign Crew Member a Ride Into Space
articles.content_orig:
China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station .
Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit.
The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.
Hours earlier, crowds of people attended a send-off ceremony, with many holding up their phones to capture the moment.
The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during their mission, official Chinese news agency Xinhua earlier reported. Ali will conduct a photosynthetic cyanobacteria experiment in orbit during his short-term mission before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, it said.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.
"Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space," he said on X on Tuesday.
The joint flight is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.
While this was the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, Tang has flown on two previous missions and is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, national broadcaster CCTV said.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.
In front of reporters, those efforts were reflected in Ali's Mandarin proficiency. He cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.
"It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said in Mandarin.
Speaking in English, he said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the moon, Mars and beyond.
In May, China launched Shenzhou 23 , which carried three astronauts, including one crew member who was set to remain in space for about a year.
China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The U.S. is widely seen as China's main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

articles.title_orig: Libyan army vows retaliation after 2 naval officers die of wounds from Ukrainian drone attack
articles.title_zh: Libyan army vows retaliation after 2 naval officers die of wounds from Ukrainian drone attack
articles.content_orig:
Jamie Dettmer is associate editor and a foreign affairs columnist for POLITICO.
Ukraine’s attack on a Russian warship in a Libyan port was a striking military success. It may also have broken international law.
“An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia’s war” was how Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy lauded Sunday’s sinking of the Merkury, one of Russia’s most advanced corvettes, docked at the time in Benghazi. Ukraine’s leader proudly announced on his Telegram channel that the operation, involving seven Ukrainian-made sea drones, had also disabled a Russian cargo ship suspected of transporting weapons.
From a military perspective the operation was indeed another one of Ukraine’s audacious commando missions. It was reminiscent of the derring-do spirit of Winston Churchill’s “Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare,” better known as the Special Operations Executive, which mounted commando raids along the French coast, causing havoc and raising British wartime morale during WWII .
In fact, the day before, while visiting Kyiv, Britain’s defense secretary Wes Streeting had coincidentally compared Zelenskyy to Britain’s iconic wartime leader.
The comparison was ironic given the circumstances. Despite Churchill’s impatience and determination to take the fight to the enemy, the wartime prime minister was careful to avoid breaching the laws of armed conflict at sea. He didn’t, for example, order British warships to sink the German cruiser Admiral Graf Spee when it was cornered in Montevideo after the Battle of the River Plate. The trapped warship’s captain ultimately decided to scuttle the ship.
But Zelenskyy wasn’t so restrained this week. According to international legal scholars, the attack likely violated international law as well as Libya’s sovereignty. The country’s eastern administration, based in Benghazi, has called on the U.N. to investigate the sinking as well as “reports regarding the presence of Ukrainian personnel, experts or military units” in western Libya.
The Libyans would have a good case if they lodged a complaint with the International Court of Justice, said David Letts, a retired Australian naval officer and now director of the military law program at the Australian National University in Canberra. “Unless you’re wanting to mount an argument that Libya is somehow involved in the conflict between Ukraine and Russia and neutrality doesn’t apply, I’m struggling to see how this sinking sits within the law,” Letts said.
Letts is one of the authors of the Newport Manual on the Law of Naval Warfare, a compilation of legislation published and updated by the U.S. Naval War College. He says Ukraine’s Benghazi attack is “quite different when compared to their strikes against Russian vessels in the Black Sea and in Black Sea ports” in disputed and not neutral waters.
The laws of neutrality are largely based on the 1907 Hague Convention, which codified the rights and duties of non-belligerent states during armed conflicts. Under it, countries at war are prohibited from conducting attacks, blockades or mine-laying within neutral waters. In return, neutral states shouldn’t let belligerent warships turn their ports into military bases. Stays are generally limited to 24 hours, with exceptions for damage, repairs or poor weather.
“The attack was a violation of Libya’s neutrality,” said James Kraska of the U.S. Naval War College and professor of international maritime law in the Stockton Center for International Law. “An attack is lawful if it’s beyond 12 nautical miles from the coastline, but, of course, inside it’s a violation.”
“Now on the Ukrainian side, what their argument might be is that a belligerent warship ought only to stay 24 hours in a foreign neutral port. If it goes beyond 24 hours, then the warship is at risk, and Libya might not be in compliance,” Kraska, a retired U.S. Navy commander, told POLITICO. “If there’s inclement weather, or repairs are needed to make it seaworthy, then the time can be extended,” he added. Some scholars, he added, would argue that Ukraine would need to contact the Libyan authorities to find out the status.
In terms of its boldness and reach, Monday’s attack wasn’t entirely unprecedented. In March, Libyan authorities reported damage to the Russian gas tanker Arctic Metagaz while it was en route to Egypt. Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the tanker with naval drones likely launched from Western Libya. Kyiv neither confirmed nor denied its involvement.
The governments of Sudan, Mali and Niger have also accused Ukrainian special forces of mounting operations in their countries, where Russian mercenary soldiers are present. Kyiv has denied those allegations.
This time, though, Kyiv has proudly admitted sinking the Merkury in a neutral port. Why? And does the breach of law on neutrality actually matter? Zelenskyy’s office didn’t respond to questions from POLITICO on the sinking, including as to whether it had sought counsel from senior government law officers before approving the attack, and whether it had notified Libyan authorities beforehand to request the ship leave Benghazi.
In the past, when questions of neutrality have arisen or Ukraine has been accused of breaching the laws of warfare, Kyiv has said this is no time for niceties as it is the aggrieved nation. When a U.N. monitoring mission in 2023 alleged abuse of Russian POWs, for example, the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry thanked the mission for documenting Russia’s violations but pushed back on the claims against Kyiv, arguing: “We consider it unacceptable to place responsibility on the victim of aggression.”
Former U.K. diplomat Tim Willasey-Wilsey, now a fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a defense think tank in London with close ties to Ukraine’s defense ministry, says that when it comes to the sinking of the Merkury, he doesn’t believe the legal issues are important. “Who gives a stuff, really, you know? To be honest, I don’t think the legality particularly matters.”
He said the biggest political risk for Kyiv is diminishing the “remarkable degree of Western support for Ukraine,” and so was reassured when Wes Streeting came out so quickly in support. The attack, he said, reflected desperation in Ukraine, where ballistic missile attacks are devastating civilian infrastructure, itself a violation by Russia of international law. “The war is clearly getting more and more visceral, and I think the timing of the Benghazi attack is testimony to the sense of desperation that there is now in Kyiv.”
But turning a blind eye to the Benghazi attack only adds to the erosion of international legal norms and the undermining of the post-1945 “rules-based international order,” which Moscow and Beijing have little time for. It makes the seas more dangerous.
Letts stressed how important it is for countries like Ukraine to stick to what’s legal. “I wonder what the attitude would be if this vessel had been docked in Genoa or Southampton, say, rather than Benghazi,” he added. “I think there’s an element here of ‘It was only over there, so it doesn’t really matter.’”
“Having built up a body of law that tries to protect victims of armed conflict, tries to limit the scope of armed conflicts, are we willing to wave goodbye to all of that?” he asked. “Are we willing just to have total warfare with all the rules gone and to say, ‘The last 100 years or so are a waste of time. Do whatever you want.’ I don’t think we are.”

articles.title_orig: Starbucks Is Said to Engage Banks for Sale of Japan Business
articles.title_zh: Starbucks Is Said to Engage Banks for Sale of Japan Business
articles.content_orig:
Discussions are at an early stage and may not result in a deal. Starbucks operates around 2,000 coffee shops in Japan, a country where it has been established for more than three decades
Share your coffee, cocoa and tea related stories with us at [email protected] .
MILAN – Starbucks is working with Citigroup and Morgan Stanley ahead of the possible sale of its operations in Japan – one of the American chain’s largest markets outside the United States – in a deal in which the Seattle-based company’s Japanese business could be valued at up to $3 billion.
The news was reported by Bloomberg yesterday, Tuesday 24 November. Starbucks is reportedly gauging interest from strategic and financial investors ahead of a formal process that could begin by the end of the year.
Discussions are at an early stage and may not result in a deal. Starbucks operates around 2,000 coffee shops in Japan , a country where it has been established for more than three decades.
It has recently had to contend with increasingly fierce competition from local rivals and rising operating costs. In a statement to Reuters, a company spokesperson said that Starbucks continually assesses the best structure for its customers creating value for shareholders.
Should it go ahead, the deal in Japan would mirror the strategic approach already adopted by Starbucks in China , where the company agreed to sell a majority stake in its Chinese business to private equity firm Boyu Capital at a $4 billion enterprise value.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia stock stumbles again after Jensen Huang's spectacular comeback rally
articles.title_zh: Nvidia stock stumbles again after Jensen Huang's spectacular comeback rally
articles.content_orig:
When voters headed to the polls and flipped Congress this month, they sent a clear message to Washington: They wanted change.
Voters wanted curbs on the technology industry's outsized power in Washington and CEOs cozying up to President Donald Trump to sway politics in their favor.
The Monday reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at Trump's urging may be exactly the opposite of what voters voiced with their ballots.
"This whole ordeal only reinforces what Americans already believe about a broken political system that stands up for Big Tech CEOs and not the American people," Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of The Tech Oversight Project, told CNBC.
Republicans are warning that Trump's unwavering support for the embattled artificial intelligence chip kingpin could further alienate voters.
"The data were so clear in the election that people don't trust big tech. The corruption message, I think, resonated a lot for Democrats in the election, and I think this sort of thing isn't helpful to Republicans in Congress who are going to be running again in two years," said Brendan Steinhauser, a GOP strategist and CEO of The Alliance for Secure AI Action , who had warned that AI data centers could be a "sleeper issue" in the lead-up to the 2026 midterms.
Before and after Election Day, voters were clear about their concern, which centered on data centers.
A Pew Research Center survey published in October found that 44% of voters considered AI very important to their vote. An NBC News exit poll found that 56% of voters said AI and data centers were crucial or a major factor in their vote for Congress. And in states including Texas, data center opposition forced GOP lawmakers who once welcomed development to change their positions.
There's a lot for tech CEOs to cheer under Trump, who was welcomed with open arms following a period of tough enforcement under President Joe Biden , and many reasons to align with the administration, said Sarah Kreps, a political scientist and professor at Cornell University who studies the intersection of technology and national security.
Chief among the reasons for celebration are the market's AI-driven gains since Trump's 2025 inauguration and his light-touch approach to tech regulation . The Nasdaq has gained nearly 21% from Jan. 17, 2025, the last trading day before the inauguration, and Tuesday's close.
"In the end, this looks like a calculated risk that the people and interests Trump prioritizes benefit more from a stable, rising market than the administration loses from the optics," Kreps said of Huang's reinstatement, adding that the Republican Party will be left to "bear the consequences" in 2028.
Outside the rarefied air of Silicon Valley and the White House, there is scant support for Huang's comeback after a series of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that critics say could have jeopardized national security and undermined the U.S.'s advantage in the AI race.
Trump sought to allay those fears this week when he told CNBC that he assured the board that Huang posed no national security threat. Instead, Trump used concerns over the CEO giving his talents to China as a major rationale behind the reinstatement push.
"The bigger threat would be losing the brain power of somebody like Jensen," Trump told CNBC this week. "That would be a threat to me. That would be a far bigger threat than anything we're talking about."
Haworth said the reinstatement raises concerns over how Huang's access to Trump benefits the company's business interests, especially as the U.S. investigates chip smuggling into China.
At the same time, Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick's perceived slowness to clamp down on illegal advanced AI chip sales to China, as well as his family's financial ties to Nvidia via Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial firm his sons now run, have drawn further congressional scrutiny.
"Voters are struggling with the high cost of living. They're angry about the corruption they see and a system that has been working more and more for the wealthy and well-connected, and making it harder and harder on working families," Rep. Suzan DelBene , D-Wash., chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee told CNBC.
"Corruption is an affordability issue. When they see money and favors going in places that don't help support working families, that's an affordability issue for them," DelBene said.
As Republicans try to rebuild after being routed in the midterms, the kind of leniency Trump has shown to Huang could backfire, GOP strategists told CNBC.
"Voters are tired of 'rules for thee, but not for me.' Most Americans have to live with the consequences of their decisions," said Brittany Martinez, executive director of Principles First, a center-right grassroots advocacy organization. "If you're a billionaire with the president's ear, apparently the White House will help you get your job back. That's exactly the kind of double standard that makes people wonder whose side this administration is on."
Marc Short, former chief of staff to Vice President Mike Pence and chair of Advancing American Freedom, the conservative think tank Pence founded, told CNBC that the Trump administration's involvement in Huang's reinstatement "sends a very terrible signal."
"I think it's consistent with the administration taking ownership in 41 separate private companies, to now feel that they can determine to the board who should be the CEO of one of America's biggest companies," he said.

articles.title_orig: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
articles.title_zh: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Chen Jining, Communist Party Secretary for Shanghai attends a deliberation on the government work report, on the sideline of the National People's Congress at the Beijing Hotel, March 6, 2025. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.
The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.
A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.
The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.
The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.
"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."
The recent Politburo purges highlight how much Chinese politics depend on shifting circumstances, with even officials with qualities that Xi apparently valued being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University based in Washington.
"On paper," they appear to be "individuals Xi would appreciate," Torigian said, but afterward, "we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them."
Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.
The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been viewed as a stepping stone to China's top leadership. The country's former President Jiang Zemin, its current premier, Li Qiang, and Xi himself previously held the position.
Chen has served as Shanghai party secretary since 2022. He previously held senior positions in Beijing's municipal government and headed the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

articles.title_orig: Russia’s Grip On Crimea Much Weaker After Key Waterways Blocked
articles.title_zh: Russia’s Grip On Crimea Much Weaker After Key Waterways Blocked
articles.content_orig:
Home » Russia’s Grip On Crimea Much Weaker After Key Waterways Blocked
Ukraine’s major attack on the Kerch Bridge, combined with a less-reported October strike on a bridge over the Don River, has effectively cut off the Sea of Azov. This makes it much harder for Russia to resupply Crimea.
8 years ago, on the 25th November 2018, Russia blocked the waterway under the Kerch Bridge to prevent Ukrainian ships accessing the Sea of Azov. At the time, despite a 2003 agreement guaranteeing free access to both countries to the Sea of Azov, Russia held the cards. Today the waterway under the Kerch bridge is again blocked, but this time it is different.
Ukraine’s successful attacks on the Kerch Bridge on 17th November have effectively severed the road link between Crimea and Russia. But it is much worse than that for Russia.
The collapsed bridge is blocking the shipping canal under the bridge. Combined with another less well-publicised attack on the rail bridge in Rostov on Don on 10th October , this greatly contributes to cutting off Crimea. At the time the strike was reported to have affected rail traffic, but the greater impact was on shipping. The port of Azov has essentially ceased operations. So both bridge attacks stop vital waterways at either end of the Sea of Azov, making it much harder for Russia to resupply Crimea.
The Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014, is effectively becoming an island. The overland supply routes through the occupied territories in southern Ukraine are under constant and substantial air threat. They also rely on smaller bridges at both ends of the route which have repeatedly been disabled by Ukrainian strikes. And at the southern end, the Kerch Road bridge to Russia is now destroyed. The rail bridge still stands, but it is damaged and remains under threat.
Ukraine has been increasing its attacks along the road connection to northern Crimea. The M14 highway has been colloquially nicknamed the ‘ highway of death ’. Several low bridges have been struck at its eastern end near Rostov, and the Chonhar bridge at the Crimea end has been seriously damaged in previous attacks. Traffic is currently being rerouted across a temporary crossing.
The simplistic solution for Russia is to switch to shipping to keep the peninsula supplied. But this is where the strikes on the two bridges, combined with a major drone campaign against shipping starting in June, greatly impede this. That campaign which used mid-strike aerial drones to target shipping, codenamed Operation ‘Molochka’ meaning ‘ Moscow will fall because of Crimea ’, saw around 300 vessels hit . Shipping had already significantly decreased in the Sea of Azov even before the Kerch bridge was felled.
The October attack on the rail bridge over the Don River in Rostov also plays a part. Ukrainian strike drones appear to have targeted the lifting mechanisms, with footage of the attack showing impacts high up in its steel lattice structure. Information seen by Naval News indicates that the bridge was disabled, meaning that it can no longer be raised to allow ships to pass underneath. Only small vessels have passed under it since the attack.
So with both ends now blocked, the Sea of Azov has effectively become a closed lake. Only ships already in it will be able to be used for resupply from the east. And they will rely on road and rail networks to be loaded in ports. There are also only two viable ports, Krym and Kerch, on the Sea of Azov side of Crimea. Both are near the Kerch bridge and subject to frequent strikes. Maritime logistics in the Black Sea are similarly restricted.
The increasingly strained logistics, combined with fuel shortages and major energy outages make Russia’s grip on Crimea appear ever weaker. The peninsula is likely to become more of a focus over the coming months.

articles.title_orig: US tells citizens to leave Iran, warns hostilities could escalate fast
articles.title_zh: US tells citizens to leave Iran, warns hostilities could escalate fast
articles.content_orig:
Washington warned citizens across the Middle East to exercise heightened vigilance after Iran attacked US assets in Bahrain and Kuwait and Yemen's Houthi forces struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district, wounding 11 people.
The US Virtual Embassy in Iran issued a security alert on Wednesday citing the attacks and warning that hostilities could escalate rapidly.
It said Iran, the Houthis and other groups aligned with Tehran may target US interests and citizens in the region, including companies and institutions.
"Do not travel to Iran for any reason. United States citizens should leave Iran immediately," the alert said.
A Houthi attack on Tuesday struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district, wounding 11 people, Saudi Arabia's Civil Defence said.
Bahrain's Interior Ministry said Tehran's attacks on Saturday wounded two people and caused a fire at a civilian industrial facility.
US citizens in the region were urged to monitor airline and airport operations and prepare for possible flight cancellations and airspace closures.
The alert also warned that rules for crossing Iran's land borders and entry conditions in destination countries may change at short notice.
Citizens were advised to avoid demonstrations, large gatherings and areas with a heavy police presence, and to stay alert in places associated with the US.
In the event of air attacks, the alert said citizens should keep away from doors, windows and debris, keep their mobile phones charged and follow instructions from local authorities.
It directed citizens to register with the US State Department's information system to receive security updates.
The US and Iran have had no diplomatic relations since 1980. Switzerland acts as the protecting power for US interests in Tehran, and the alert named the US interests section at the Swiss embassy there as a point of contact for citizens needing assistance.

articles.title_orig: China space station receives Pakistani astronaut on 'historic mission'
articles.title_zh: China space station receives Pakistani astronaut on 'historic mission'
articles.content_orig:
China on Wednesday launched the Shenzhou 24 spacecraft with three astronauts — two Chinese and a Pakistani — sending the first foreign crew member to its space station .
Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo, 51, and Wu Yi, 39, after the craft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China on Wednesday morning. It successfully separated from a rocket and entered its predetermined orbit.
The launch marked the first joint flight involving Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program.
Hours earlier, crowds of people attended a send-off ceremony, with many holding up their phones to capture the moment.
The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during their mission, official Chinese news agency Xinhua earlier reported. Ali will conduct a photosynthetic cyanobacteria experiment in orbit during his short-term mission before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou 23 spacecraft, it said.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his best wishes to the astronauts ahead of their mission.
"Pakistan-China friendship is surpassing the heights of the Himalayas in its journey to outer space," he said on X on Tuesday.
The joint flight is part of an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025.
While this was the first spaceflight for Ali and Wu, Tang has flown on two previous missions and is set to become the first astronaut to board the Tiangong space station three times, national broadcaster CCTV said.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Tang said that differences in language, culture and psychology had made learning to work together more challenging on this mission, but that both sides' efforts were paying off.
In front of reporters, those efforts were reflected in Ali's Mandarin proficiency. He cited a line of Chinese poetry about climbing one story higher to see farther.
"It's like my daily training. Day after day, reaching new heights," he said in Mandarin.
Speaking in English, he said he hoped the next chapter of space cooperation between the two countries would go from one astronaut in one flight to multiple joint flights and to the moon, Mars and beyond.
In May, China launched Shenzhou 23 , which carried three astronauts, including one crew member who was set to remain in space for about a year.
China is preparing for its first crewed lunar landing by 2030. The U.S. is widely seen as China's main space rival, with NASA aiming to land astronauts on the lunar surface in 2028.

SHENZHEN, China — President Trump has begun an extraordinary visit to Shenzhen, where he is set to join the leaders of Russia and China — two of Washington’s principal geopolitical rivals — for an unprecedented trilateral summit Thursday.
Chinese President Xi Jinping personally welcomed Trump on the tarmac upon his arrival, reciprocating a rare honor Trump extended to him during his September visit to Washington.
All three leaders attended a dinner alongside other regional heads of government on Wednesday night, participating in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.
The trilateral meeting will be the first of its kind by leaders of the United States, Russia and China, three nations with the world’s largest nuclear arsenals.
But while Trump has embraced a strategy of diplomatic engagement with historic foes, the three leaders enter the meeting with starkly different agendas.
Russian President Vladimir Putin hopes to secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine. Trump says he would like to discuss a nuclear arms control agreement and his war in Iran. And Xi aims to present China as a superpower on the international stage, capable of forging world peace.
Meeting with Putin before Trump arrived, Xi said that China’s relationship with Russia had remained as steadfast “as a rock through wind and rain.”
The two sides, he said, would pursue a “multipolar world” — a vision for a global balance of power that would see American influence weakened across Europe and Asia.
A new rule tightening loopholes in U.S. export controls sends a dual message to Beijing ahead of Thursday’s summit.
Trump, for his part, has hedged on his expectations of the summit, signaling resolve against China ahead of his arrival here.
On Monday, the Trump administration tightened export controls on semiconductor chips essential to artificial intelligence development, closing loopholes aimed at curbing Chinese efforts to circumvent restrictions — a move that Trump acknowledged might be an “insult” to Xi before the meeting.
Chinese officials said Wednesday afternoon that Beijing reserved the right to retaliate.
“In essence, the United States is simultaneously trying to find limited avenues of cooperation with China while trying to clamp down on their access to critical parts of the AI supply chain, which doesn’t set up the conditions for productive dialogue,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
Trump also met in Manila on Tuesday with fellow members of the Quad — India, Japan and Australia — in a show of resolve toward Beijing.
“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in the Philippines.
“We continue to protect peace through strength,” he added.

articles.title_orig: Asia’s markets dive as return of Nvidia’s Huang fails to quell AI doubts
articles.title_zh: Asia’s markets dive as return of Nvidia’s Huang fails to quell AI doubts
articles.content_orig:
By IMOGEN GARFINKEL - SENIOR FOREIGN NEWS REPORTER
Published: 02:32 EST, 25 November 2026 | Updated: 03:38 EST, 25 November 2026
Nvidia's re-instated chief executive Jensen Huang told employees on Tuesday that he had violated some of the company's code of conduct and made 'some terrible mistakes', one person familiar with the matter said.
Mr Huang, who co-founded Nvidia 30 years ago, said he was in therapy and acknowledged it was not acceptable to have violated aspects of the firm's code of conduct, the person said.
Nvidia shares closed 5.9 per cent lower as Monday’s historic rally, sparked by Mr Huang's re-instatement, lost steam.
The pullback came as investors shifted their focus to the political and governance risks surrounding his return.
His resignation last week over revelations of extramarital affairs, one with an alleged Chinese spy, roiled markets and unsettled the AI ecosystem reliant on the chipmaker's technology and funding.
Mr Huang apologised while disagreeing with reports that he had been an abusive boss, the New York Times reported, citing a livestream of the meeting it had reviewed.
Mr Huang also rejected claims that he returned because he was a 'tech bro' and 'above the law', and said he returned because Nvidia's board had evaluated facts and was assured that there was no threat to national security, NYT and Bloomberg News reported.
Mr Trump, while on a call with an American news outlet, took credit for getting Mr Huang back at the helm.
Reinstated CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, reacting to the ovation from employees upon his return to the company headquarters in Santa Clara, California
Huang said he was in therapy and acknowledged it was not acceptable to have violated aspects of Nvidia's code of conduct
Nvidia said ​in a statement on Monday that based on US government input, the board was confident that 'Huang's re-instatement poses no national security risk', a claim backed by Mr Trump.
US lawmakers from both parties sharply criticised Nvidia's decision, saying Congress should scrutinise the circumstances surrounding Mr Huang's return.
'The reinstatement itself raises as many questions as it answers. His return removes a major uncertainty, but what it leaves behind is an overhang on how Nvidia's governance is viewed,' said Dan Sheehan, director of portfolio management at Telos Wealth Advisors.
'There are also questions... about how involved the government will be in Nvidia, and about governance of conduct internally given the stance the reinstatement implicitly took. Those don't get resolved by a soaring stock price.'
In an interview with the New York Post, Mr Trump said that he's willing to pardon Mr Huang if necessary but that he believes the re-installed Nvidia chief executive should be fine without one.
Mr Trump also told the New York Post that Nvidia's success was essential to the US retaining an edge in AI and that he's even open to the company giving the American government an equity stake, noting Intel handed more than 10 per cent of its stake last year.
'I thought about it. I said, "You know, maybe I should do it", but I didn't bring it up at this point. It's probably not too late,' Mr Trump told the New York Post.
Nvidia and the White House could not immediately be reached for comment outside regular business hours.
Both Mr Huang and Nvidia are facing a host of state and federal probes and reviews, including from the FBI, the Justice Department and the US Securities and Exchange Commission.
Huang, 63, was greeted by chants of 'Jensen, Jensen' as he strolled into the microchip manufacturer's offices in Santa Clara, California on Monday morning
Trump posted a meme on his Truth Social showing Huang holding up a red bra in a wild re-imagining of the iconic photo after Trump was shot by a would-be assassin in 2024
A public Senate hearing is set for December 3, where Mr Huang is due to testify, while the board's own investigations into potential foreign intelligence efforts, national security and export controls are still underway.
'Now that the dust is beginning to settle, people are taking a more critical look at (Nvidia's) decision... They (board) put themselves at a tremendous ethical and legal risk by the decision they made,' said Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management.
Mr Huang's upcoming testimony is also an 'enormous risk to the company', he said.
The surge on Monday propelled Nvidia back into second place among the world's most valuable companies, behind Apple, although the stock remains almost 31 per cent below its October 6 record high.
AI-related companies, including chipmakers and data-centre stocks, rose sharply as well, while the benchmark S&P 500 added more than $2.8trillion in market value.
'As incredible as Monday was, I don't take it as a sign we're out of the woods... a market that can rise $3 trillion on one headline can fall just as fast on another,' Telos' Sheehan said.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk Confirms Free Starlink Hardware for Eligible Americans as SpaceX Gives Up $738 Million in Federal Grants
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk Confirms Free Starlink Hardware for Eligible Americans as SpaceX Gives Up $738 Million in Federal Grants
articles.content_orig:
Ever since SpaceX’s Starlink won nearly $700 million in Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment (BEAD) awards it immediately began quibbling about aspects of the government program. Now, the low-Earth-orbit (LEO) broadband provider has decided it’s not going to accept its BEAD funding. Instead, it’s struck a deal with the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) to remain in the BEAD program but to provide its equipment for free in the areas where it won BEAD awards.
NTIA Administrator Arielle Roth issued this statement: “To accelerate BEAD deployment and simplify the process for serving locations across the country, NTIA and SpaceX have engaged in discussions to streamline implementation of the program. As a result, SpaceX has agreed to abide by BEAD service and performance testing requirements at all locations awarded under a state or territory’s Final Proposal at no cost to the BEAD program.”
As part of the deal, NTIA has created a “model agreement” for states to use if they want to continue to work with SpaceX.
According to a statement from NTIA, some states have been slow to sign sub-grant contracts with LEO providers. And the fact that there are 56 states and territories in the BEAD program has caused distress for LEO providers, “imposing a patchwork of obligations.”
Of course, many fiber providers and fixed wireless access (FWA) providers are also dealing with a patchwork of state obligations with BEAD, but Roth didn’t address that.
Yesterday, NTIA announced a new model agreement for state broadband offices to work with LEO providers.
NTIA said states should use this model agreement with a LEO provider that agrees to meet BEAD service and performance testing requirements at locations awarded to it, but that elects to decline BEAD subsidies.
According to NTIA, the model agreement ensures that the LEO operator will provide service at BEAD-required speeds, provide customer premises equipment to BEAD subscribers at no additional cost, comply with performance testing requirements, offer a low-cost service option, and submit semi-annual reports detailing performance and subscription statistics at BEAD broadband-serviceable locations (BSLs).
The model agreement was presented to the state broadband offices yesterday. Now, they must decide if they want to go in this direction with SpaceX and use the model agreement or decline to use it and identify another provider to serve applicable locations at a comparable cost.
States that choose not to proceed with the model agreement will be responsible for identifying a provider to serve the applicable locations at a cost comparable to the cost approved under the state’s original Final Proposal.
Finding an alternate provider at a comparable cost to a satellite operator will be nearly impossible for already-stressed state broadband officers , given the fact that Starlink and Amazon Leo were always far cheaper than fiber or FWA.
Another catch is that by allowing SpaceX to remain in the BEAD program with a $0 award, other broadband competitors are prevented from bidding in those eligible locations.
Fiber Broadband Association President and CEO Gary Bolton issued a statement today, saying, “Requiring states to find another provider at a comparable cost to Starlink’s original award makes that choice impractical in many communities. We urge NTIA to let states reopen these locations to competition in the next BEAD funding round, and give them the flexibility to put the remaining $21 billion in BEAD funds toward infrastructure that will serve rural communities for decades.”
In terms of the next BEAD funding round, Bolton was referring to the decision by NTIA in September to open another bidding round given the fact that there remains about $21 billion in left-over funds. This surplus is largely due to the fact that the Trump administration altered the program to favor lower-cost LEO satellite providers.
Bree Maki, executive director of Minnesota's Office of Broadband Development, said, "NTIA hosted an all-state director webinar yesterday notifying us, and we received their new model agreement with SpaceX late last night. We (Minnesota) have not heard anything from SpaceX."
She said each state is going to have to evaluate the model agreement provided by NTIA and work with their state legal council on state-specific rules and contracting.
"I would emphasize that this is another program change states are being asked to navigate in accordance with NTIA requirements," said Maki. "Minnesota remains committed to supporting providers still participating in the program to the best of our ability, while working to serve the unserved and underserved locations NTIA has determined eligible for BEAD. People in these areas have been waiting far too long."
Fierce has reached out to several state broadband offices and will update this story with their comments.

articles.title_orig: Trump Says He’s Open To Pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—Who Reportedly Still Holds Security Clearance
articles.title_zh: Trump Says He’s Open To Pardoning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang—Who Reportedly Still Holds Security Clearance
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — President Trump told The Post in an exclusive interview that he’s willing to pardon Jensen Huang if necessary — but that he believes the reinstalled Nvidia CEO should be fine without one and should “tell the truth” to Congress when he testifies next week .
Trump, who pressured the company’s board to take Huang back, took a victory lap after Nvidia’s stock surged Monday — inspecting the latest numbers at the Resolute Desk during the interview and noting the price ticked up in the afternoon, partially reversing a slump earlier Tuesday.
“That’s not bad, went down a couple of points,” Trump commented while reviewing the numbers. “It really picked up at the end.”
Huang doesn’t need to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights to avoid self-incrimination when he sits for an interview with the House Foreign Affairs Committee next Tuesday and appears before a hearing of the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday, Trump added.
“I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people,” Trump said.
“I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person.”
Asked about a pardon for any potential crimes , Trump said, “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress blasted the reinstatement of Huang before getting answers on whether he was a national security threat or violated export controls on shipping chips to communist China.
Angry lawmakers previewed a tough grilling of Huang with Louisiana Republican Sen. John Kennedy predicting Huang will plead the Fifth to avoid self-incrimination amid potential criminal prosecution.
Trump said that he hadn’t learned granular details of additional affairs that Huang admitted to before being restored as CEO — after the firestorm over his tryst with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang (no relation) and at least two company employees.
The president said, however, that it’s his understanding that Huang wasn’t sleeping with any other women with questionable links to Beijing.
“No, not from what I understand. I didn’t really get into it very much, to be honest with you. But no, from what I understand, no,” Trump replied.
He also said he didn’t know precisely how many affairs Huang fessed up to as part of his restoration.
“I really didn’t get into that. I got into the business of chips, much more than the business of sex,” Trump joked.

The president said that Nvidia’s success was essential to the US retaining an edge in artificial intelligence — and that he’s even open to the company giving the American government an equity stake, noting Intel handed over 10% of its value last year.
“I thought about it. I said, ‘You know, maybe I should do it,’ but I didn’t bring it up at this point. It’s probably not too late,” Trump said.
The president said he intervened to restore Huang, including by giving assurances that he faced no issues from the executive branch, because if Nvidia picked “the wrong person” to replace Huang, “that would be a terrible thing for our country in many ways.”

Gold prices fell ​on Wednesday as ​the dollar firmed, while ​market participants awaited key US inflation data due later in the day for clues on the Federal Reserve's interest-rate trajectory.
Spot gold fell 1% to $3,519.94 per ounce ⁠by ‌0708 GMT. Prices had hit a 14-month low ⁠on Friday. US gold futures for December delivery dropped 1.2% to $3,519.00.
"The recent decline was mainly driven by a selloff in the equity market because investors needed cash to pay for ‌margin calls. As of now, markets continue to remain in consolidation mode until further signals," said ANZ analyst Soni Kumari.
"Key drivers ​like the US dollar being quite strong remains one of the key headwinds for gold," she said.
The dollar index, which measures the greenback against six peers, rose 0.2%, making greenback-priced bullion more expensive ⁠for buyers overseas.
Asian stocks tumbled as fresh US tariff threats hit sentiment and a ‌tech-led rally fizzled, with the region's chip-heavy markets bearing ‌the brunt of the selloff.
The US Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Index, a key gauge closely watched by the central bank as it targets a 2% inflation rate, is ⁠due at 1330 GMT.
Markets are fully pricing in a 25-basis-point rate ⁠increase at the Fed's policy meeting in December, according ⁠to CME's FedWatch tool.
Higher rates increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion.
US consumer confidence increased more than expected in November, touching ​its highest level in nearly two ‌years, amid optimism over labour market conditions and the overall economy following this month's midterm elections.
"We expect gold's downward pressure to eventually reverse, although the recovery could remain muted into early 2027 before gaining momentum," analysts at OCBC said in a ​note.

articles.title_orig: Putin says retaliation ‘inevitable’ after Ukraine hit Russian oil plants
articles.title_zh: Putin says retaliation ‘inevitable’ after Ukraine hit Russian oil plants
articles.content_orig:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has told Russian President Vladimir Putin to "stop complaining" over attacks on Russian refineries, saying Putin could end Kyiv's strikes on the oil facilities by bringing an end to the Kremlin's nearly five-year-long war.
His comments come shortly after Russia's president told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin on Tuesday that Ukraine continues to attack refining facilities despite U.S. President Donald Trump 's appeal to refrain from doing so.
"I would like to note that retaliatory action from our side is inevitable. Everyone must be aware of that," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency Tass .
In September, Trump called on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks were " hurting the world " as fuel supply disruptions from the wars in Ukraine and Iran propelled U.S. diesel prices to a record high. Moscow welcomed Trump's push for Ukraine to halt strikes on Russia's diesel-producing facilities at the time.
"If Putin doesn't like Ukraine's strikes on his oil refineries, he can order an end to the war," Ukraine's Sybiha said Tuesday via social media.
"If he doesn't want his military vessels hit, he can order an end to the war. Not to mention the 432,000 Russian soldiers he has lost on the battlefield this year without coming any closer to the goals of his invasion. Clearly, he doesn't care about them. Stop complaining. End the war," he added. CNBC could not independently verify the figures.
In July, the Center for Strategic and International Studies estimated that about 1.4 million Russian troops were killed, wounded or went missing between the start of the full-scale invasion in Feb. 2022 and June 2026, with more than 30,000 casualties a month in the first half of this year.
Ukraine has stepped up attacks on Russian critical targets in recent weeks, damaging Putin's prized Crimea bridge , striking a Russian cargo ship in the Baltic Sea and destroying one of Russia's newest ships at a Libyan port .
Kyiv has also targeted Russian energy infrastructure . Zelenskyy said earlier this month that Ukraine's long-range strikes had disabled more than 55% of Russia's oil-refining capacity, describing this as a "justified response to Russia's refusal to de-escalate and its strikes on our energy infrastructure."
Ukrainian drones reportedly struck two major Russian oil refineries in Russia's Samara region overnight, triggering fires at both facilities.
Satellite images published in late October also showed black smoke rising from multiple fires at Rosneft's Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in southern Russia following a suspected Ukrainian drone attack.
Putin on Tuesday said Russia's fuel market situation remains "challenging" and called on government officials and oil executives "to continue reacting promptly to the supply-demand relationship for fuel across the whole territory of Russia," according to Interfax .
Ukraine's allies have warned the country faces another winter of blackouts and freezing temperatures amid escalating Russian energy strikes.

articles.title_orig: Trump Accounts hit major milestone as family contributions surpass $1 billion
articles.title_zh: Trump Accounts hit major milestone as family contributions surpass $1 billion
articles.content_orig:
Former Deputy Treasury Secretary Michael Faulkender analyzes the potential expansion of Trump accounts for adults. He also weighs in on the challenges China's domestic economy is facing.
Contributions from friends and family members to Trump Accounts have surpassed $1 billion, marking a major milestone for the children's investment program as Americans prepare for the holiday season.
More than 3 million friends and family members have contributed to individual Trump Accounts — investment accounts established for children under 18 — surpassing $1 billion in personal contributions, according to a Treasury Department statement provided to FOX Business.
Combined with philanthropic gifts and the federal government's $1,000 seed contributions for eligible children, total assets deposited in Trump Accounts have now surpassed $9 billion.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent praised the milestone Tuesday, saying Americans were increasingly taking advantage of the program to invest in children's financial futures.
HOUSE DEM TARGETS 4 COMPANIES IN PROBE INTO TRUMP JR-LINKED 1789 CAPITAL
President Donald Trump speaks during the Trump Accounts Launch Summit in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Jan. 28, 2026. (Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty Images / Getty Images)
"The American people are investing in Trump Accounts with a generosity that represents the finest instincts of our national character," Bessent said in a statement.
"President Trump wanted to make it especially easy to contribute to Trump Accounts, and friends and families across the country are seizing that opportunity to help the next generation build wealth from day one," he continued.
Bessent added that each contribution helps bring the promise of long-term financial security within reach of American children.
He also said that President Donald Trump had joined millions of Americans making personal contributions to individual accounts.
"This week, the President himself joined the millions of Americans who have made personal donations to individual Trump Accounts," Bessent said.
BANK OF AMERICA CEO HONORED AT $32M FUNDRAISING EVENT AGAINST ANTISEMITISM
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent praised the milestone after contributions from friends and family members to Trump Accounts surpassed $1 billion nationwide. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images / Getty Images)
Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children under 18 with valid Social Security numbers.
Children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, are eligible for a one-time $1,000 seed contribution from the federal government.
While Trump Accounts have been created for eligible children under 18, parents and guardians must claim the accounts before they can manage them or enable contributions.
With the holiday season approaching, friends and relatives can contribute directly to a child's Trump Account once it has been claimed.
According to Treasury, contributors can use a QR code generated through the child's Trump Accounts app to make deposits.
TOP TRUMP CRYPTO MEME COIN HOLDERS AWARDED WITH EXCLUSIVE DINNER EVENT
President Donald Trump's children's investment account program surpassed $1 billion in contributions from friends and family members, according to the Treasury Department. (Alex WROBLEWSKI / AFP via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Family members and friends can contribute up to a combined $5,000 per year to each account, while employers can contribute up to $2,500 annually, subject to the overall $5,000 limit.
The latest milestone follows the Treasury Department's announcement last month that approximately 70 million Trump Accounts had been established for eligible children.
Major philanthropic donors have also pledged support to the program, including Michael and Susan Dell, who pledged approximately $6.25 billion to provide $250 to 25 million eligible children.

President Donald Trump displays a signed document alongside Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano in the Oval Office, pictured next to a graphic of the new $1,000 Trump Account notice being sent to parents of newborns. (Social Security Administration)
Parents and guardians can claim their children's accounts through the official Trump Accounts app. Additional information is available at TrumpAccounts.gov.

articles.title_orig: China's Shenzhou-24 carries Pakistan's first astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali into space
articles.title_zh: China's Shenzhou-24 carries Pakistan's first astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali into space
articles.content_orig:
China launched its Shenzhou-24 space mission on Wednesday carrying three astronauts to its Tiangong space station, including Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreigner to join a Chinese crewed space mission.
Beijing said it hopes the flight will strengthen ties with Islamabad, as the two countries mark 75 years of co-operation in space.
Speaking to reporters at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center, Ali said he was "carrying the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis".
The mission, which also comprises of commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi, took off at 08:18 (00:18 GMT) from the Gobi desert. Minutes later, it was declared a "complete success".
While in space, the Shenzhou-24 crew will carry out experiments and test technology in fields like aerospace medicine, combustion and study the effects of space on living organisms.
They will also study how the space environment affects aging, with the hope of developing new ways to prevent and treat age-related vascular diseases.
Ali will conduct studies on photosynthesis in bacteria and the effects of radiation and microgravity - a very weak gravity in space - on seeds.
The former fighter pilot will return to Earth after a short stay, with two other Chinese crew members who have been at the space station since May.
Tang and Wu will spend six months at Tiangong space station along with Zhu Yangzhu, a member of the Shenzhou-23 crew, which lifted off in May this year. Zhu has been studying how the human body adapts to long periods in space.
The Shenzhou-24 is also a diplomatic moment for Beijing.
China has poured billions of dollars into its space programme and its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.
It is now keen to show the world that the station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.
This also comes at a time when Beijing is trying to establish itself as a major alternative to the US-led space programme, with a bold goal to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030.
For Pakistan, which does not have its own spacecraft to send astronauts to space, being invited to be a part of this mission is significant.
Ali and Khurram Dawood, the other candidate to reach the final stage in the Shenzhou-24 crew selection, were trained in China and had worked in Chinese space stations under the supervision of Chinese experts.
Mastering the Chinese language was one of his "biggest challenges", Ali said, according to Pakistani media.

articles.title_orig: This nation had a security pact with China. It’s just signed a deal with a US ally instead
articles.title_zh: This nation had a security pact with China. It’s just signed a deal with a US ally instead
articles.content_orig:
The Solomon Islands has signed a "historic" treaty with Australia, after reportedly telling China it was ending a controversial security pact signed in 2022.
At a press conference in Canberra on Wednesday, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale said the new treaty would ensure that Australia was the Pacific nation's "security partner of choice".
In 2022 the Solomon Islands, then under the leadership of now-Opposition Leader Manasseh Sogavare, signed a security and policing pact with Beijing .
There were fears the pact gave China a crucial military and strategic foothold in the Pacific amid a battle for influence in the region with the US.
On Tuesday, Australian media outlets reported that Honiara had told Beijing it would not renew the pact, understood to be expiring in April 2027.
Wale told reporters on Wednesday there were "ongoing discussions" with China but he was "unable to talk about" the pact, because of a non-disclosure agreement.
He said the treaty with Australia provided a reset after several years in which the Solomon Islands had been a point of "uncertainty and doubt in the region".
"Those days are done, gone," Wale said.
Albanese said the treaty would strengthen the two countries' security partnership.
"Backing our Pacific neighbours is an investment in Australia's own security and our own prosperity."
"We'll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions."
On Tuesday China's foreign ministry spokesman, Guo Jiukan, did not confirm or deny that the pact had been terminated.
"There is no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation in cooperation between China and Pacific island countries, including the Solomon Islands," Guo said.
The pact was never publicly released, but leaked excerpts revealed it gave China extensive involvement in security and policing including deploying its own officers to the Solomon Islands, and allowed it to establish a quasi military base.
It was a "massive coup" for Beijing, said Lowy Institute Research Fellow, Dr Connor Graham, but its unprecedented scale sparked alarm in the Pacific and the West.
Wednesday's treaty had delivered "an enormous win for Canberra", and "closes the loop" on a series of security deals Canberra signed with Pacific nations in the wake of the Solomons-China pact.
"That [China pact] was the thing that put fear in the hearts of diplomats in Washington and Canberra," he told the BBC.
William Yang, the International Crisis Group's Senior Analyst for North East Asia, said the end of China's "flagship" Pacific deal and the signing of the new treaty also reaffirmed the Pacific's "longstanding consensus-based decision-making model, especially in the security space".
Under the new treaty, the Solomon Islands commits to prior consultation with Australia on critical infrastructure and to ensure any security cooperations are with Pacific Islands Forum members. China is a dialogue partner but not a member of the forum.
Honiara also commits to its sensitive infrastructure remaining "free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access", and to not permit its territory to be used for any foreign military or security base.
The Solomons will receive support for its free education system and sports programs, improved visa arrangements, and support for the expansion of affordable and renewable energy and infrastructure development.
Earlier this week the ABC reported the package promised more than A$980m (£460.7m, $648,000) in additional funding, citing leaked text messages. The BBC has not independently verified the text messages.
Wale visited Australia to sign the treaty, accompanied by two dozen Solomons MPs. He and Albanese said the size of the delegation demonstrated that the treaty had strong support from the country's parliament, after years of political instability - largely driven by disagreement over the country's relationship with China .

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang says he’s thankful for second chance at Nvidia employee meeting
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang says he’s thankful for second chance at Nvidia employee meeting
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang made a triumphant return to the semiconductor giant in an all-hands meeting Tuesday morning, apologizing to staff for his conduct during his previous stint at the company’s helm and vowing to do better this time around.
No company has impacted the world as deeply or profoundly as Nvidia, Huang said, according to an Nvidia employee who attended the meeting. Huang called the company’s story the most interesting in the world.
According to the individual, Huang expressed contrition for his past behavior and was adamant that employees should follow the company’s code of conduct. The AI hardware leader resigned from the company on Nov. 12 amid mounting scrutiny about alleged romantic relationships with subordinates and Alice Huang, a former executive at Singaporean cloud computing company Megaspeed. According to U.S. intelligence officials, Alice Huang is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset.
He also said that he has been regularly attending therapy and that he had been deeply embarrassed about recent events, the source said. The CEO was met with an overwhelmingly positive reception, even receiving a standing ovation, according to the source.
Huang’s return marked a nearly unprecedented case of corporate whiplash. After a wave of reports emerged stating that Huang had been involved in extramarital relationships — potentially with someone accused of being a Chinese intelligence asset — Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a letter sent to Nvidia employees and shared online on Nov. 8.
“To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me,” Huang wrote at the time. “I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.”
Huang issued a personal statement on Nov. 17, expressing remorse but professing his admiration for and dedication to Nvidia. Huang founded the semiconductor designer in 1993 and grew it into what was once the world’s most valuable company.
“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” Huang wrote in that statement. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”
Less than a week later, Nvidia’s board announced that Huang would return to the company — backed by “input from senior levels of the United States government” that essentially guaranteed “Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
Huang said in Tuesday’s meeting that President Donald Trump supported the company. “President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang said, according to the Nvidia employee.
Huang said that Nvidia was an apolitical company. Huang added that he returned as CEO because the board — and not the government — had wanted him to be reinstalled.
The meeting, which kicked off around 9:30 a.m., lasted around an hour, according to the source, who added that Huang exited to the Foo Fighters’ song “Times Like These.”
Jean Lee reports with NBC News’ Social Newsgathering team in Los Angeles. She previously reported for the NBC News investigative unit.
Jared Perlo is a technology reporter focused on AI for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Amnesty calls for ICC genocide probe over Israel's impact on births in Gaza
articles.title_zh: Amnesty calls for ICC genocide probe over Israel's impact on births in Gaza
articles.content_orig:
In a report on women and girls in Gaza, the NGO denounces the consequences of restrictions on and shortages of reproductive healthcare. It calls on the ICC to investigate
Amnesty International is accusing Israel of imposing measures in Gaza that have prevented Palestinian women from conceiving or carrying their pregnancies to term. In a report published Wednesday, the organization says the repeated effects of these measures raise serious concerns about an intent to prevent births.
It adds, however, that it cannot conclude with certainty that this was the Israeli authorities’ objective.
The NGO calls on the International Criminal Court (ICC) to include violations of reproductive health and gender-based crimes in its investigation into possible acts of genocide. Under the UN Convention, measures intended to prevent births within a group can constitute an act of genocide if they are taken with the intent to destroy that group, in whole or in part.
The report draws in part on 228 remote interviews conducted between October 2023 and October 2026. Amnesty reports cases of women and girls killed or injured while seeking care or in a maternity ward.
Two emergency responders described shots fired in early 2026 at a woman about to give birth and the ambulance sent to pick her up, near the “yellow line.”
Amnesty says that restrictions and shortages have limited access to fertility treatment and obstetric care. A lack of equipment, anesthetics, and medications to treat hemorrhaging has reportedly made it harder to monitor pregnancies and manage childbirth, resulting, according to the organization, in miscarriages, stillbirths, and sometimes fatal complications.
The report also notes that no in vitro fertilization clinics are currently operating in Gaza and that thousands of stored embryos and gametes have been destroyed.
In response, COGAT, the Israeli agency responsible for coordinating civilian affairs in the Palestinian territories, accused Amnesty of spreading “Hamas’s false narratives.” It told AFP that more than 27,000 tons of medical equipment and medicines had entered Gaza since the ceasefire began in October 2025, and that 35 hospitals were operational, including facilities specializing in women’s health and fertility care.
The report also addresses the use of hospitals by Palestinian armed groups. Amnesty says it gathered evidence of hostages being held and Palestinians being tortured in healthcare facilities, but found no evidence to support Israeli allegations that hospitals had served as Hamas command centers.

articles.title_orig: TSA anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week
articles.title_zh: TSA anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week
articles.content_orig:
The Transportation Security Administration expects to screen roughly 17.6 million passengers nationwide between Tuesday and next Monday, projecting more than 3 million travelers on the Sunday after Thanksgiving alone.
The Transportation Security Administration announced on Tuesday that it anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week, vowing to help families reach their loved ones for the holiday "as safely and securely as possible."
The agency said it expects to screen about 17.6 million air travelers across the country between Nov. 24 and 29, including more than 3 million passengers at U.S. airports on the Sunday after Thanksgiving.
"TSA is prepared to handle the increased passenger volumes expected during the Thanksgiving holiday travel period while maintaining our focus on security," TSA Administrator David Cummins said in a statement. "I am grateful to the TSA employees who will work throughout the holiday to help ensure the traveling public reaches their destinations safely. A little preparation by passengers can help make the screening process more efficient for everyone."
The TSA urged people traveling over Thanksgiving week to arrive at the airport at least two hours before domestic flights and three hours before international flights.
FAA ISSUES GROUND DELAY AT CHICAGO O'HARE DUE TO 'EQUIPMENT OUTAGE'
The Transportation Security Administration announced on Tuesday that it anticipates nearly 18 million air travelers during Thanksgiving week. (Peter Zay/Anadolu via Getty Images / Getty Images)
Travelers should give themselves extra time for parking, airline check-in, baggage drop-off and security screening, the agency said.
"At TSA, our highest priority is security," Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said in a statement. "While our partners at the Federal Aviation Administration and the airlines oversee other aspects of your journey, TSA is responsible for screening everyone safely and securely. DHS is ready to help ensure millions of American families can reach their loved ones as safely and securely as possible over the coming days. I also want to thank our patriotic TSA employees for working tirelessly to deliver on our homeland security mission during this busy holiday season."
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) also predicted the busiest holiday skies in 16 years for Thanksgiving week.
The FAA said there were more than 417,000 forecast flights over a nine-day holiday period. Tuesday was set to be the busiest travel day, with 52,345 flights expected to take off.
For flights home after Thanksgiving, 44,265 flights are scheduled on Saturday, while 50,314 are set for Sunday, the FAA said.
DUFFY SOUNDS ALARM OVER AGING FAA SYSTEM AFTER NATIONWIDE AIR TRAVEL SHUTDOWN
The TSA said travelers should give themselves extra time for parking, airline check-in, baggage drop-off and security screening. (REUTERS/Aaron Schwartz / Reuters)
"Our air traffic controllers and safety professionals are working around the clock to keep Americans moving during what is expected to be the busiest Thanksgiving travel week in 16 years," FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said in a statement. "The growing demand for air travel makes it more important than ever to continue modernizing our air traffic control system and build a national airspace system for the 21st century."
The agency added that weather conditions could impact flights throughout the week.
On Tuesday, low ceilings were forecast to affect flights along the West Coast. Thunderstorms were possible across Florida and the Gulf Coast on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Rain could affect flights across the Southeast, including Atlanta, on Wednesday before moving into the Mid-Atlantic later in the day. Rain and wind are expected to impact the Northeast on Thanksgiving Day.
The anticipated heavy travel for Thanksgiving week comes after the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13 due to telecommunications equipment failures, interrupting travel for more than a million travelers during the nearly four-hour delay.
The TSA said it expects to screen more than 3 million passengers at U.S. airports on the Sunday after Thanksgiving. (Erin Hooley/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service / Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO READ MORE ON FOX BUSINESS
The FAA also issued a ground stop on Tuesday afternoon for regional flights arriving at Chicago-O'Hare due to an equipment failure with the airport's runway surface radar. The ground stop was lifted after about an hour, and a subsequent ground delay was canceled about an hour after that.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Tuesday that Americans "can rest assured we will be on the clock 24/7 to get families to their destinations safely and on time."
"As millions of Americans prepare to hit the road or take to the skies to spend the holiday season with their loved ones, the Trump Administration's message is clear: your safety is our number one priority. From standing up a Tiger Team to ensure a seamless travel experience for fliers to using a successful new platform to predict and address congestion in the airspace, we’ve taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancelations," he said in a statement.
